title: Pain au chocolat
subtitle: laminated croissant dough filled with dark chocolate
excerpt: Pain au chocolat is a rectangle of laminated croissant dough wrapped around two dark chocolate batons and baked until deeply browned. You get flaky, buttery layers that shatter at the outside and soften to a honeyed chew closer to the chocolate. Watch the lamination temperature: if the butter warms and smears into the dough, the layers vanish.
sourceNotes: Croissant dough lamination is documented in French patisserie manuals from the late 19th century onward. The pain au chocolat format is a standard product of French boulangeries. The lamination method described here follows established professional pastry practice.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze before the final prove. Arrange on a lined tray, freeze solid, then transfer to a freezer bag. To bake: remove the night before, arrange on a lined tray, and leave to prove overnight at room temperature. Egg wash and bake from room temperature as directed.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The dough requires an overnight rest after the first chill and ideally a further overnight cold prove after shaping. Plan across two days.

baking.bakeTemperatureNote: Conventional oven, 200 degrees Celsius. Fan oven: 185 degrees Celsius. Bake for 16 to 18 minutes.

glossaryTerms.definition: The technique of folding a block of cold butter into a dough in repeated turns to create hundreds of distinct alternating layers. During baking, moisture in the butter converts to steam and forces the layers apart, producing the characteristic flaky, open structure of croissants and pain au chocolat. The butter must remain cold and solid throughout; if it melts into the dough the layers merge and the pastry bakes heavy and bready.

The butter block used in laminated pastry. It is beaten and shaped into a flat slab so that it can be enclosed in the dough and rolled without breaking. High-fat European-style butter (83 percent or above) is standard because it is more plastic and less likely to crack when cold.

The initial yeast dough before butter is incorporated. The detrempe must be chilled until firm before the lamination begins, so that dough and butter are at the same pliable-but-not-soft consistency and roll together rather than one breaking through the other.

A laminated yeasted dough. The presence of yeast distinguishes it from puff pastry: during the final prove the yeast generates gas inside the layers, giving croissant-family pastries their open, irregular crumb alongside the flaky crust.

content.text: Combine the flour, salt, sugar, and yeast in a large bowl. Keep the salt and yeast on opposite sides of the bowl until you start mixing, as direct contact can impede fermentation. Add the cold milk and the softened butter. Mix to a shaggy dough, then knead for 3 to 4 minutes until smooth. The dough should be soft and slightly tacky but not sticky. Do not over-knead: excessive gluten development at this stage makes the dough resistant to rolling later.

Shape the dough into a flat rectangle, wrap tightly in cling film, and refrigerate for at least 1 hour (or overnight). The cold milk and short chill keep the dough from proving significantly at this stage. A chilled detrempe rolls with less spring-back and stays cool against the butter during lamination.

Remove the butter from the refrigerator. Place it between two sheets of baking parchment or in a zip-lock bag. Beat it with a rolling pin to flatten and make it pliable, then fold and beat again until you have shaped it into a slab approximately 18 cm x 18 cm and about 1 cm thick. The butter should flex without cracking and feel cold but not rigid. If it is too cold and shatters when you roll it, leave it at room temperature for 5 minutes and try again. If it is too soft and leaves an oily residue on the paper, return it to the refrigerator for 10 minutes. Return the beurrage to the refrigerator until you are ready to laminate.

On a lightly floured surface, roll the detrempe into a rectangle approximately 38 cm x 20 cm. Centre the beurrage slab on the lower half of the dough. Fold the upper half of the dough down over the butter so the butter is completely enclosed. Press the edges to seal. You now have a parcel with butter inside.

Roll the parcel away from you into a long rectangle, roughly 60 cm x 20 cm, using firm, even strokes. Work quickly. For the first double fold (book fold): fold the top quarter of the dough down to the centre, fold the bottom quarter up to meet it, then fold the whole thing in half along the centre line. You now have four layers. Wrap in cling film and refrigerate for 30 minutes.

Remove the dough from the refrigerator. Orient it with the open edges to your left and right (not toward you). Roll again to approximately 60 cm x 20 cm. Perform a second double fold exactly as before. Wrap and refrigerate for another 30 minutes.

Repeat the roll and double fold for the third and final time. After three double folds you have 64 layers of butter. Wrap and refrigerate for at least 1 hour, or overnight. The longer rest at this stage relaxes the gluten, reduces spring-back when rolling to final thickness, and lets the dough firm up before cutting.

Remove the dough from the refrigerator. On a lightly floured surface, roll to a rectangle approximately 40 cm x 30 cm and about 4 to 5 mm thick. Use a ruler and a sharp knife or bench scraper to trim the edges cleanly; ragged edges have compressed layers that do not rise as well. Cut into 8 rectangles, each approximately 10 cm x 15 cm.

Place one rectangle in front of you with the long side running left to right. Lay one chocolate baton across the short end nearest to you, about 2 cm from the edge. Roll the dough over the chocolate once. Place a second baton against the roll. Continue rolling the dough away from you to enclose both batons in a tight cylinder. The seam should be underneath. Place on a lined baking tray. Repeat with the remaining rectangles.

Leave the shaped pastries at room temperature, loosely covered, for 2 to 3 hours. They are ready to bake when they have puffed noticeably, look slightly wobbly when the tray is gently shaken, and the individual layers are visible at the cut ends. Do not prove in a warm oven or near a heat source: above 25 degrees Celsius the butter begins to melt, causing greasy pools at the base and lost layering.

Heat the oven to 200 degrees Celsius (conventional). Apply a thin, even coat of egg wash to the top and sides of each pastry using a pastry brush. Avoid letting the egg wash drip down the cut layers at the ends: it glues the layers together and reduces rise.

Bake for 16 to 18 minutes. The pastries are done when they are a deep mahogany brown all over, including on the sides and base. The base should sound hollow when tapped. Pale golden pastries will be doughy inside; full colour is essential. Transfer to a cooling rack immediately.

attrs.problem: Butter leaked out onto the tray during baking and the pastries look greasy rather than flaky
attrs.avoid: Avoid proving in a warm environment. If the butter reaches 25 degrees Celsius or above during the prove, it begins to melt into the dough and leaks out in the oven.
attrs.fix: The lamination may also have been done with butter that was too warm. Next time, refrigerate the dough for 20 to 30 minutes between each fold and check that the butter remains cold and solid throughout.

attrs.problem: The layers are barely visible after baking and the pastry is bready rather than flaky
attrs.avoid: Avoid rolling too aggressively, which smears the butter into the dough rather than keeping it in distinct layers.
attrs.fix: Check that the beurrage was the same consistency as the dough when lamination began. If the butter is too cold it shatters and breaks through the dough; if too warm it smears. Both result in lost layers.

attrs.problem: The pastry is very pale on top but burnt on the base
attrs.avoid: Avoid using a dark-coloured baking tray, which absorbs heat quickly and scorches the base before the top has browned.
attrs.fix: Stack two baking trays together to create a buffer of insulating air, or use a lighter aluminium tray. If the tops are still pale by the time the base is done, move the tray to the top shelf for the last 3 minutes.

attrs.problem: The dough springs back and tears when rolling to final thickness
attrs.avoid: Avoid skipping the resting periods between folds. The gluten tightens with each fold and must be given time to relax before rolling further.
attrs.fix: If the dough is resisting, wrap it and refrigerate for 20 minutes. The cold also relaxes the gluten slightly. Never force a resistant dough: tearing destroys the layers.
